newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarians expected to deal blow to ruling party.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarians expected to deal blow to ruling party.

text.p: Bulgarians voted on Sunday in a presidential election run-off expected to deal a decisive blow to the ex-communist ruling party which lagged in last week's first round.
Opinion polls predict a comfortable win for opposition candidate Petar Stoyanov, who last Sunday finished 17 points ahead of Culture Minister Ivan Marazov, candidate of the governing Socialists.

But the key to the Balkan country's future lies less with the president than with an International Monetary Fund mission discussing terms for the release of a $115 million credit that is vital to prevent Bulgaria defaulting on its foreign debt.

Opinion polls give Stoyanov between 57 and 64 percent of the vote, firmly ahead of his rival, but many Bulgarians more concerned with how to make ends meet during the winter are disillusioned with politicians of any persuasion.

"I can't see any difference between Stoyanov and Marazov," said Naidenka Mihova, an elderly woman collecting rubbish in central Sofia on Sunday morning. She said life had been cheaper before the end of communist rule in 1989.
Many votes last week went to protest candidates and the turnout on Sunday is expected to be lower than the first round's 63 percent.

Under Bulgaria's post-communist constitution, the president is a largely ceremonial figure and real power lies with parliament where Prime Minister Zhan Videnov's divided Bulgarian Socialist Party has a clear majority.

Videnov said last week changes in the cabinet or the party leadership now would only make matters worse but party reformists predict a split after the presidential poll which could lead to early parliamentary elections.
Neighbouring Romania and Yugoslavia, also voting on Sunday, are themselves battling economic crises. But reform laggard Bulgaria has the lowest foreign investment in the region.

Union of Democratic Forces candidate Stoyanov, an advocate of a market economy and closer ties with the European Union and NATO, polled 43.93 percent in the first round, short of the absolute majority he needed to win.

The maverick populist head of the Bulgarian Business Bloc, George Ganchev, won the lion's share of protest votes last week, polling 21.8 percent. He has declined to back either second round candidate.
IMF mission leader Anne McGuirk, who is due to meet Videnov on Sunday, told reporters the Fund would evaluate Bulgaria's reform performance before deciding on further funding.
The IMF has twice postponed the $115 million second tranche of its standby credit, saying the government must fulfil its pledges to close loss-making state enterprises and speed up privatisation.

In a last-minute bid to convince the Fund of its commitment to reform, the Bulgarian National Bank on Thursday started bankruptcy proceedings over eight out of nine banks placed in receivership in September.

Economic austerity and the threat of bread and fuel shortages in the coming winter have thrown a shadow over an election campaign already marred by bombings and violence culminating in the October 2 assassination of former prime minister Andrei Lukanov.
On Wednesday a home-made bomb destroyed the car of Haralambi Anchev, a member of the Central Electoral Committee.
